title: The dawn chorus is on
body: Robins and sparrows sing loudest in this first hour. Stop for ten seconds {where} and count the voices.

title: White-throated Sparrows are back
body: They flew down from Canada for the winter. Listen for their thin whistled song in the bushes.

title: Pigeons are off to breakfast
body: They leave the ledges in little groups and land wherever crumbs were dropped last night.

title: Squirrels are burying nuts
body: Morning is their busiest time. Watch one dig, drop, pat it down and look around to check who saw.

title: Sparrows are dust-bathing
body: Look by the curb {where}. They roll in dry dirt to keep their feathers clean and bug-free.

title: Pigeons are sunbathing
body: One wing tilted up, eyes half closed. The warmth helps them shake out parasites and it just feels good.

title: Squirrels are napping
body: After the morning rush, many curl up in their leafy nest, called a drey, until the afternoon.

title: Starlings are gathering
body: They line up on the wires {where}, chattering, before heading to a shared roost for the night.

title: Crows are commuting home
body: In fall, crows fly across the city at dusk to sleep together in big roosts.

title: Pigeons are back on the ledge
body: Pairs settle in side by side. Same ledge, same partner, every night.

title: Raccoons start their rounds
body: The night shift is up. They check the same spots {where} in the same order most nights.

title: Moths are at the streetlights
body: Bright lights pull them off course. Every porch light you switch off helps.

title: Birds are migrating in the dark
body: Right now songbirds are flying south over the city, calling softly to stay together.

title: Juncos are on their way
body: These little gray snowbirds are flying down from Canada and will spend the winter hopping under your hedges. White-throated Sparrows are arriving too.

title: The chimney swifts have left
body: The tiny birds who zipped over the rooftops all summer are flying to South America. Monarchs are passing through on their way to Mexico.

title: The dawn chorus is at full volume
body: Robins start before sunrise and everyone else joins in. Stand still {where} and see how many songs you can pick apart.

title: White-throated Sparrows are singing goodbye
body: Their whistled Oh sweet Canada fills the bushes before they fly north in May.

title: Mourning doves are cooing
body: That slow, soft hoo-OO-oo-oo is a love song. Look for two plump birds side by side on the wire.

title: Pigeons are courting
body: He puffs up his neck, spins in a circle and bows. She acts like she hasn't noticed. Watch the sidewalk {where}.

title: Sparrows are moving in
body: They stuff grass and feathers into any gap they find: signs, traffic lights, holes in old brick.

title: Squirrel babies are tucked in
body: New kits are hidden up in the drey. Mom dashes out for food and back again, over and over.

title: Red-tails are sitting on eggs
body: High on a ledge or a tall tree {where}, a hawk is keeping eggs warm in a big nest of sticks.

title: Robins sing the day out
body: They're the first to sing in the morning and some of the last at night. Listen for a cheery, rolling song.

title: Crow families are nesting
body: Last year's young crows stick around to help feed the new chicks. Family first.

title: Starlings are dressed up
body: Glossy purple and green feathers, bright yellow beaks. They're singing from rooftops {where}, car alarm impressions included.

title: Raccoon moms are working overtime
body: With babies back in the den, moms are out longer than usual, sometimes even in daylight.

title: Opossum moms carry the family
body: Tiny babies ride in her pouch now. In a few weeks they'll cling to her back instead.

title: Birds are flying north in the dark
body: Right now songbirds are passing over the city on their way to their summer homes, calling softly to stay together.

title: The chimney swifts are back
body: These tiny birds just flew in from South America. Look up for cigar-shaped birds zipping and twittering over the rooftops.

title: The juncos are heading north
body: The little gray snowbirds who spent the winter under your hedges are flying back to Canada. White-throated Sparrows are leaving too.

title: Robin kids are on the lawn
body: Spotty-chested fledglings hop around while their parents bring them worms. They look lost, but they're fine.

title: Sparrow kids are begging
body: That fluttering, chirping racket {where} is fluffy young sparrows chasing their parents for breakfast.

title: Pigeons are on their next family
body: Many pairs raise several families a summer. Mom sits on the eggs at night, dad takes the day shift.

title: Squirrels are splooting
body: On hot days they flatten out belly-down on cool shade or stone to cool off. It's called splooting.

title: Monarchs are on the milkweed
body: They lay one tiny egg at a time on milkweed leaves, the only plant their caterpillars can eat.

title: Young starlings are everywhere
body: Plain brown and noisy, they follow their parents across every patch of grass {where}.

title: Swifts are zipping over the roofs
body: Chimney swifts catch bugs on the wing until the light fades. Listen for their high twittering {where}.

title: Young hawks are calling
body: That long, wheezy scream is a young red-tail asking its parents for dinner while it learns to hunt.

title: Crow families are heading in
body: Noisy young crows follow their parents to the trees for the night, begging the whole way.

title: Moths are out in force
body: Warm nights mean hundreds of kinds are flying. Every porch light you switch off helps them.

title: Raccoon families are on their rounds
body: A mom leads a line of youngsters along the fence {where}, teaching them the route.

title: Young opossums are on their own
body: Freshly independent, they're exploring yards and alleys for the very first time. Give them space.

title: Monarchs are here
body: The great-great-grandchildren of last fall's travelers have made it back north. Look for big orange butterflies at the flowers.

title: The baby birds are moving out
body: Young robins, sparrows and starlings are leaving their parents' care. By fall you won't be able to tell them from the grown-ups.

title: Crows are leaving the roost
body: Thousands slept together last night. Now they're spreading out across the city, family by family.

title: Sparrows are puffed up
body: They fluff their feathers into little round balls to trap warm air. Check the hedge {where}.

title: Pigeons are huddled on the ledge
body: Pressed together, feathers fluffed, waiting for the sun to reach their side of the building.

title: Juncos are hopping under the hedge
body: Little gray birds with white bellies, scratching for seeds. When they fly, white tail feathers flash.

title: Squirrels are chasing
body: Those wild spirals around the tree trunk {where} are squirrels courting. Babies will come in early spring.

title: Red-tails are courting
body: Pairs soar in wide circles together. Sometimes one dives at the other and they touch talons in the air.

title: Starlings are wearing their stars
body: In winter their dark feathers are covered in white speckles. Look for them lining up on the wires {where}.

title: Crows are commuting to the roost
body: Long lines of crows cross the sky at dusk, all heading to the same few roosts to sleep together.

title: Doves are soaking up the last sun
body: They sit puffed up on the wires facing the sunset, catching every bit of warmth before night.

title: Raccoons are sleeping in
body: On the coldest nights they stay curled up in the den. They don't hibernate, they just skip a few shifts.

title: Opossums are keeping warm
body: Their bare ears and tails feel the cold, so on freezing nights they stay tucked away.

title: Squirrels are tucked in the drey
body: Curled up in a leafy nest, tail wrapped around like a blanket. Sometimes two share for warmth.

title: More gulls are here
body: Gulls from the north come down to spend the winter on the city's rivers and harbor. Look for big mixed groups on the piers.

title: The monarchs are in Mexico
body: The butterflies who passed through in fall are clustered by the millions on fir trees in the mountains, waiting for spring.
